expansion:
The patient’s enophthalmos and loss of sensation over the lower eyelid, cheek, lateral nose, upper lip, and upper teeth is classic for an orbital‑floor (blow‑out) fracture that compresses the infra‑orbital canal. The deck states that "INFRAORBITAL NERVE ANAESTHESIA: Involving the lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, upper teeth and gums if the fracture involves the infraorbital canal" (L25, slide 22). Enophthalmos is listed as a possible sign of an orbital‑floor fracture (L25, slide 20). Therefore the nerve most likely injured is the infra‑orbital nerve, option B.

The supra‑orbital nerve supplies the forehead, scalp and upper eyelid; it does not innervate the lower lid, cheek, or upper lip, so it cannot explain the described anesthesia pattern (not taken from the course material).

The facial nerve is a motor nerve that controls the muscles of facial expression and does not provide cutaneous sensation to the mid‑facial region; thus it would not cause the sensory deficits noted (not taken from the course material).

The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, pharynx, and tonsils, and has no branches to the orbit or mid‑face, making it an implausible cause of the presented signs (not taken from the course material).
objective: Identify the nerve damaged in an orbital floor fracture that produces infra‑orbital sensory loss and enophthalmos
